claims.text: The target material is a single-phase, cast or arc-melted high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are major constituents.
The proposed intervention is a uniform 5–10 μm alumina coating deposited by PVD or CVD.
An alumina-based coating will inhibit high-temperature oxidation of a titanium- and nickel-dominated HEA.
Inhibiting oxidation with the coating will preserve the alloy's microstructural integrity.
Preserving microstructural integrity with the coating will improve elevated-temperature mechanical performance relative to an uncoated specimen.
An intact alumina layer will protect grain boundaries and phase stability from oxygen ingress and high-temperature degradation.
At high temperature in an oxidizing atmosphere, titanium is prone to forming deleterious oxides.
Titanium oxides formed during exposure can weaken grain-boundary bonding and reduce mechanical strength.
The alumina coating will act as a diffusion barrier that minimizes oxygen penetration.
Minimizing oxygen penetration will suppress surface and grain-boundary oxidation.
The coating will reduce phase segregation during high-temperature exposure.
The coating-mediated suppression of degradation will retain solid-solution strengthening.
Coated specimens will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength and ultimate tensile strength than uncoated specimens.
Coated specimens will have better elevated-temperature ductility than uncoated specimens.
Coated specimens will exhibit less oxidation-induced degradation than uncoated specimens.
The hypothesis is applicable to alloys containing more than 20 at.% titanium and more than 20 at.% nickel under oxidizing conditions from approximately 600 to 1000 °C.
The predicted coating benefit may not generalize to inert or reducing atmospheres.
The magnitude of improvement and the effects of adhesion, thermal-expansion mismatch, and coating-induced microstructural modification are uncertain.
